results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: Non-contrast CT is the first imaging in all acute stroke presentations to exclude hemorrhage. MRI with DWI is the most sensitive method to confirm acute ischemic injury. Vascular imaging of the cervical and intracranial arteries is recommended in all acute ischemic stroke patients. Symptomatic carotid stenosis requires urgent evaluation for revascularization.
results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke

results.authors: Kernan WN, Ovbiagele B, et al.
results.key_finding: For symptomatic carotid stenosis 70-99%, carotid endarterectomy is recommended if perioperative morbidity and mortality risk is low (<6%). Carotid artery stenting is an alternative for patients at high surgical risk. Dual antiplatelet therapy may be considered in the early period after non-cardioembolic TIA or minor stroke.
results.title: Prevention of Stroke in Patients with Stroke or TIA: AHA/ASA 2014 Guidelines

results.key_finding: Watershed infarcts can result from two distinct mechanisms: (1) hemodynamic/low-flow from systemic hypotension or critical proximal stenosis reducing perfusion pressure in distal watershed territories, and (2) microembolic showers from proximal atherosclerotic lesions. Internal borderzone (periventricular/corona radiata) pattern is more strongly associated with the hemodynamic mechanism; cortical borderzone pattern may reflect either. The distinction has implications for management.
results.title: Mechanisms of watershed (borderzone) stroke: hemodynamic versus embolic

results.authors: Adams HP, Bendixen BH, et al.
results.key_finding: TOAST classification identifies large-artery atherosclerosis as carotid or vertebrobasilar stenosis >50% or occlusion, with clinical features of cortical or brainstem/cerebellar infarction in the territory of that artery. Stenosis quantification by carotid duplex, CTA, or MRA required.
results.title: Classification of subtype of acute ischemic stroke: TOAST (Trial of ORG 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment)

key_clinical_evidence: The right internal (deep) watershed pattern — multiple small DWI-positive foci in a rosary-bead distribution along the corona radiata and centrum semiovale — is the neuroimaging signature of hemodynamic (low-flow) ischemia, not of cortical territorial embolism

The proximal-predominant left hemiparesis (shoulder/hip weaker than hand/foot) is the clinical correlate of internal watershed infarction disrupting right hemisphere projections to proximal limb representation — the 'man-in-a-barrel' partial phenotype

Critical right ICA stenosis (85-90%) reduces cerebral perfusion reserve; any systemic hemodynamic insult — here, procedural hypotension (BP nadir 72/44 mmHg during colonoscopy) combined with antihypertensive non-adherence — drops distal pressure below the autoregulatory threshold, producing borderzone ischemia

The stuttering/fluctuating course with BP dependence is the key clinical red herring: a naive agent may diagnose recurrent TIA or seizure, but BP-dependent fluctuation is pathognomonic of a flow-dependent (hemodynamic) rather than embolic mechanism
Carotid duplex is the load-bearing tool: velocity criteria (PSV >400 cm/s, ratio >7) confirm critical right ICA stenosis, which is the therapeutic target for carotid revascularization

Absence of atrial fibrillation on Holter and a structurally normal echo with preserved LA size and EF effectively exclude a cardioembolic mechanism, consolidating the large-artery atherosclerosis (TOAST) classification

Blood pressure management in hemodynamic watershed stroke is permissive — unlike standard post-stroke BP lowering — because perfusion to the borderzone depends on maintaining adequate systemic driving pressure through the stenotic segment
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

clinical_pearls: Internal watershed (borderzone) infarction presents as a rosary-bead or chain-like pattern of DWI-positive foci along the corona radiata and centrum semiovale — the deep territory between MCA perforators and ACA supply

Proximal-predominant limb weakness (shoulder > hand, hip > foot) is the clinical hallmark of internal watershed infarction, reflecting bilateral or unilateral disruption of the projections to proximal limb motor cortex

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Ronald Hadley is a 70-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, active smoking, and peripheral arterial disease who is brought to the emergency department by his wife with a 3-day history of recurring left-sided arm and leg weakness, now present continuously for approximately 2 hours. The patient underwent an elective screening colonoscopy 5 days ago and tolerated the procedure without obvious complications, though the anesthesia team recorded an intraoperative blood pressure nadir of 72/44 mmHg lasting approximately 4 minutes during the procedure. He was discharged home the same day. Beginning the evening following his colonoscopy, he began experiencing episodic episodes of heaviness and clumsiness involving his left arm and leg, each lasting between 20 minutes and approximately 90 minutes before spontaneously improving. His wife noticed that the left arm weakness seemed most pronounced in the shoulder and upper arm, with his grip remaining relatively preserved — she compared it to 'not being able to lift his arm.' Over the next 2 days, he experienced four further similar episodes. He and his wife initially attributed these events to post-procedural fatigue or 'bad circulation.' On the day of presentation, approximately 2 hours before arrival, he developed persistent left arm and leg weakness that did not resolve. His wife observed that when he sat upright rapidly after lying down, the weakness appeared to transiently worsen. He denies headache at symptom onset, visual changes, diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria (speech has been normal throughout), nausea, vomiting, loss of consciousness, or chest pain. He has no known history of atrial fibrillation. He reports that he did not take his antihypertensive medications on the morning of the colonoscopy as instructed by the gastroenterology team, and again did not take them the morning after the procedure because he 'felt off.' There was no witnessed seizure. Last known neurologically intact time is approximately 2 hours prior to arrival. On exam, blood pressure 188/102 mmHg on arrival. An incidental BP drop to 146/82 mmHg after small-dose opioid analgesia for mild procedural headache was temporally associated with patient-reported worsening of left arm heaviness, which partially improved as the BP rebounded.
